entry.title: The First Ace
entry.content:
Problem.

A standard deck of $52$ cards is shuffled and dealt one card at a time. On average, how many cards do we turn over until the first ace shows up?

Solution.

Write $n = 52$ for the number of cards and $a = 4$ for the number of aces; the other $n - a = 48$ cards we call blanks. Let $T$ be the position of the first ace. We keep $n$ and $a$ general and plug in the numbers at the end.

The deck is uniformly shuffled: every one of the $n!$ orderings is equally likely.

Method 1: One indicator per blank

The $T - 1$ cards above the first ace are exactly the blanks that come before all the aces. So

\[T = 1 + \sum_{b} I_b ,\]

where the sum runs over the $n - a$ blanks and $I_b$ is the indicator that blank $b$ is dealt before every ace.

Fix a blank $b$ and look only at the $a + 1$ cards consisting of $b$ and the $a$ aces. Shuffling these $a + 1$ cards among the slots they occupy, and leaving every other card where it is, maps deck orderings to deck orderings bijectively. So all $(a + 1)!$ relative orders of these $a + 1$ cards are equally likely, and $b$ is the first of them with probability

\[\mathbb{P}(I_b = 1) = \frac{1}{a + 1} .\]

By linearity of expectation, whether or not the $I_b$ are independent (they are not),

\[\mathbb{E}[T] = 1 + \frac{n - a}{a + 1} = \frac{n + 1}{a + 1} .\]

Method 2: The gaps are exchangeable

The $a$ aces cut the blanks into $a + 1$ gaps: $G_0$ blanks before the first ace, $G_1$ between the first and second ace, and so on, up to $G_a$ after the last ace. Then

\[G_0 + G_1 + \cdots + G_a = n - a, \qquad T = G_0 + 1 .\]

The claim is that all $a + 1$ gaps have the same distribution. A vector $(g_0, \dots, g_a)$ of nonnegative integers summing to $n - a$ corresponds to exactly one set of ace positions: the first ace sits at $g_0 + 1$, the second at $g_0 + g_1 + 2$, and so on. Each set of ace positions is realised by the same number $a! \, (n - a)!$ of deck orderings, since the aces can be arranged in their slots in $a!$ ways and the blanks in theirs in $(n - a)!$ ways. So every gap vector is equally likely. Permuting the coordinates of a gap vector gives another gap vector with the same sum, so the joint law of $(G_0, \dots, G_a)$ does not change when the gaps are permuted: the gaps are exchangeable, and in particular $\mathbb{E}[G_0] = \mathbb{E}[G_1] = \cdots = \mathbb{E}[G_a]$.

Taking expectations in the sum,

\[(a + 1) \, \mathbb{E}[G_0] = n - a, \qquad \mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{n - a}{a + 1} + 1 = \frac{n + 1}{a + 1} .\]

Method 3: Sum the tail probabilities

For an integer-valued $T \geq 0$ we have $T = \sum_{k \geq 0} \mathbf{1}{T > k}$, since the indicator equals $1$ exactly for $k = 0, 1, \dots, T - 1$. Taking expectations,

\[\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{k \geq 0} \mathbb{P}(T > k) .\]

Now $T > k$ means the top $k$ cards are all blanks. The top $k$ cards form a uniformly random $k$-subset of the deck, so for $0 \leq k \leq n - a$

\[\mathbb{P}(T > k) = \frac{\binom{n - a}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}} = \frac{(n - a)! \, (n - k)!}{n! \, (n - a - k)!} = \frac{\binom{n - k}{a}}{\binom{n}{a}} ,\]

and $\mathbb{P}(T > k) = 0$ for larger $k$. The right-hand form has its own meaning: the $a$ ace positions are a uniform $a$-subset of the $n$ slots, and $T > k$ says they all fall in the last $n - k$ slots.

Summing,

\[\mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{a}} \sum_{k = 0}^{n - a} \binom{n - k}{a} = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{a}} \sum_{j = a}^{n} \binom{j}{a} = \frac{\binom{n + 1}{a + 1}}{\binom{n}{a}} .\]

The last step is the hockey-stick identity: an $(a + 1)$-subset of ${1, \dots, n + 1}$ whose largest element is $j + 1$ is determined by its other $a$ elements, chosen from ${1, \dots, j}$, so grouping the subsets by their largest element gives $\sum_{j = a}^{n} \binom{j}{a} = \binom{n + 1}{a + 1}$. Finally

\[\frac{\binom{n + 1}{a + 1}}{\binom{n}{a}} = \frac{(n + 1)!}{(a + 1)! \, (n - a)!} \cdot \frac{a! \, (n - a)!}{n!} = \frac{n + 1}{a + 1} .\]

Method 4: Condition on the top card

Write $E(n, a)$ for the expected position of the first ace in a deck of $n$ cards with $a \geq 1$ aces. Turn over the top card.

  • With probability $\frac{a}{n}$ it is an ace, and $T = 1$.
  • With probability $\frac{n - a}{n}$ it is a blank. The remaining $n - 1$ cards are in uniformly random order and still contain all $a$ aces, so from here on it is the same game with $n - 1$ cards: $T = 1 + T’$ with $\mathbb{E}[T’] = E(n - 1, a)$.

Hence

\[E(n, a) = 1 + \frac{n - a}{n} \, E(n - 1, a), \qquad E(a, a) = 1 .\]

Small cases suggest the answer: $E(a, a) = 1$, $E(a + 1, a) = 1 + \frac{1}{a + 1}$, and

\[E(a + 2, a) = 1 + \frac{2}{a + 2} \cdot \frac{a + 2}{a + 1} = 1 + \frac{2}{a + 1},\]

which points to $E(n, a) = \frac{n + 1}{a + 1}$. Induction on $n$ confirms it. The base case $n = a$ gives $\frac{a + 1}{a + 1} = 1$, and if $E(n - 1, a) = \frac{n}{a + 1}$ then

\[E(n, a) = 1 + \frac{n - a}{n} \cdot \frac{n}{a + 1} = \frac{(a + 1) + (n - a)}{a + 1} = \frac{n + 1}{a + 1} .\]

With $n = 52$ and $a = 4$,

\[\mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{53}{5}.\]

Remark.

The tail-sum formula: for a random variable $T$ taking values in ${0, 1, 2, \dots}$,

\[\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{k = 0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T > k) = \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T \geq k) .\]

The two sums are the same sum written twice, since ${T > k} = {T \geq k + 1}$; shifting the index $k \mapsto k + 1$ turns one into the other. So it suffices to prove the second form.

Proof by indicators. For every outcome, $T$ is the number of positive integers $k$ with $k \leq T$, that is

\[T = \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} \mathbf{1}\{T \geq k\}.\]

Taking expectations term by term,

\[\mathbb{E}[T] = \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{1}\{T \geq k\}\big] = \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}(T \geq k) .\]

entry.title: Noodle Loops
entry.content:
Problem.

You have $100$ noodles in your soup bowl. Being blindfolded, you are told to take two ends of some noodles (each end on any noodle has the same probability of being chosen) in your bowl and connect them. You continue until there are no free ends. The number of loops formed by the noodles this way is stochastic. Calculate the expected number of circles.

Solution.

Let $n$ be the number of noodles ($n = 100$), so there are $2n$ free ends at the start. Every tie uses up two free ends, so after exactly $n$ ties nothing is left: the process always has $n$ steps.

Call a strand any chain of noodles that have been tied end to end but is not yet closed. A strand has exactly two free ends, just like a single noodle. At the start there are $n$ strands. When we tie two free ends, one of two things happens.

  • The two ends belong to the same strand. The strand closes into a loop and drops out of the game.
  • The two ends belong to different strands. The two strands merge into one longer strand.

Either way the number of strands goes down by exactly one. So just before the $j$-th tie is made there are $i = n - (j - 1)$ strands in the bowl and $2i$ free ends, and just after it there are $i - 1$. Counted this way, the $n$ ties are made with $n, n - 1, \dots, 2, 1$ strands present; the last tie is made with a single strand, and closes it.

Method 1: One indicator per tie

Look at the tie made when $i$ strands and $2i$ free ends are present (that is, just before this tie). Pick the first end; whichever it is, the second end is uniform over the other $2i - 1$ free ends, and exactly one of them is the other end of the same strand. So

\[\mathbb{P}(\text{this tie closes a loop}) = \frac{1}{2i - 1},\]

whatever happened before. Let $I_i$ be the indicator that the tie made with $i$ strands present closes a loop. The number of loops is $L = I_n + I_{n-1} + \cdots + I_1$, and by linearity of expectation

\[\mathbb{E}[L] = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \frac{1}{2i - 1} = 1 + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} + \cdots + \frac{1}{2n - 1} .\]

For $n = 100$,

\[\mathbb{E}[L] = 1 + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} + \cdots + \frac{1}{199} .\]

The last term is $I_1 = 1$: when a single strand is left, its two ends must be tied to each other.

Method 2: Condition on the first tie

Write $E_n$ for the expected number of loops with $n$ noodles. The first tie joins a uniformly chosen pair among $2n$ ends.

  • With probability $\tfrac{1}{2n - 1}$ the two ends belong to the same noodle. One loop is done, and $n - 1$ untouched noodles remain.
  • Otherwise two different noodles are joined into one long strand. Now there are $n - 1$ strands, each with two free ends, and the blindfolded process does not care whether a strand is one noodle or two: from here on it is exactly the game with $n - 1$ noodles.

Hence

\[E_n = \frac{1}{2n - 1} + E_{n - 1}, \qquad E_1 = 1 ,\]

and unrolling the recursion gives the same sum $E_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \tfrac{1}{2i - 1}$.

entry.title: Two Cards Far Apart
entry.content:
Problem.

A deck has $m$ suits and $s$ ranks, one card for every suit-rank combination, so $ms$ cards in total. Two cards are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that their ranks differ by more than $k$?

Solution.

Number the ranks $1, 2, \dots, s$. Only differences of ranks matter, so any consecutive numbering gives the same answer, and we do not wrap around: ranks $1$ and $s$ are $s - 1$ apart.

Write $R_1, R_2$ for the ranks of the two cards and $D := \lvert R_1 - R_2 vert$ for their difference. Since ranks are integers, “differ by more than $k$” is the same as $D \geq k + 1$, where $k$ is an integer with $0 \leq k \leq s - 1$.

Method 1: Condition on the first card

Suppose the first card has rank $r$. The second card is uniform over the remaining $ms - 1$ cards, so we count how many of them have a rank more than $k$ away from $r$.

  • Below $r$: the ranks $r’ \leq r - k - 1$. There are $r - k - 1$ of them if $r \geq k + 1$, and none otherwise.
  • Above $r$: the ranks $r’ \geq r + k + 1$. There are $s - r - k$ of them if $r \leq s - k$, and none otherwise.

Call this number of far ranks $c_r$; each far rank carries $m$ cards. The first rank is uniform on $1, \dots, s$, so

\[\mathbb{P}(D > k) = rac{1}{s} \sum_{r = 1}^{s} rac{m \, c_r}{ms - 1} = rac{m}{s (ms - 1)} \sum_{r = 1}^{s} c_r .\]

The sum $\sum_r c_r$ counts the ordered pairs $(r, r’)$ with $\lvert r - r’ vert \geq k + 1$. In the $s imes s$ grid of ordered pairs these form two triangles in opposite corners, one with $r’ - r \geq k + 1$ and one with $r - r’ \geq k + 1$, with rows of length $1, 2, \dots, s - k - 1$ each. So

\[\sum_{r = 1}^{s} c_r = 2 \cdot rac{(s - k - 1)(s - k)}{2} = (s - k)(s - k - 1),\]

and

\[\mathbb{P}(D > k) = rac{m \, (s - k)(s - k - 1)}{s \, (ms - 1)} .\]

Method 2: Get rid of the suits and count pairs of ranks

There are $ inom{ms}{2}$ equally likely pairs of cards. Look at a favourable pair. Its two ranks are different (they are more than $k \geq 0$ apart), say $r < r’$. Once these two ranks are fixed, the suits are free: $m$ choices for the card of rank $r$ and $m$ choices for the card of rank $r’$. So

\[ ext{every pair of distinct ranks is worth exactly } m^2 ext{ pairs of cards,}\]

no matter which two ranks they are. The suits contribute the same factor $m^2$ to every favourable pair, and the whole problem collapses to a question about ranks only. Writing

\[N_k := \#\{ ext{pairs of ranks } r < r' ext{ with } r' - r > k\},\]

we have

\[\mathbb{P}(D > k) = rac{m^2 \, N_k}{ inom{ms}{2}} .\]

One caution: a pair of cards with the same rank is realised by only $ inom{m}{2}$ suit choices, not $m^2$. That is why the reduction is stated for distinct ranks only; it does not bother us here, because a favourable pair never has equal ranks.

It remains to count $N_k$. Sort the pairs $r < r’$ by their difference $d = r’ - r$. For a given $d$ the pair is $(r, r + d)$ with $1 \leq r \leq s - d$, so there are $s - d$ of them. The difference must be at least $k + 1$ and at most $s - 1$, hence

\[N_k = \sum_{d = k + 1}^{s - 1} (s - d) = (s - k - 1) + (s - k - 2) + \cdots + 1 = rac{(s - k)(s - k - 1)}{2} .\]

Putting the two together,

\[\mathbb{P}(D > k) = rac{m^2 \cdot \dfrac{(s - k)(s - k - 1)}{2}}{\dfrac{ms(ms - 1)}{2}} = rac{m \, (s - k)(s - k - 1)}{s \, (ms - 1)} .\]

Method 3: First ask whether the ranks are different at all

Method 2 also says that, given the two ranks are different, every unordered pair of ranks is equally likely, since each is realised by the same number $m^2$ of card pairs. So split the event into two steps.

Step 1. Whatever the first card is, $m - 1$ of the remaining $ms - 1$ cards share its rank, so

\[\mathbb{P}(R_1 eq R_2) = 1 - rac{m - 1}{ms - 1} = rac{m (s - 1)}{ms - 1} .\]

Step 2. Conditionally on $R_1 eq R_2$, the pair of ranks is uniform over the $ inom{s}{2}$ possibilities, so

\[\mathbb{P}(D > k \mid R_1 eq R_2) = rac{N_k}{ inom{s}{2}} = rac{(s - k)(s - k - 1)}{s (s - 1)} .\]

Multiplying,

\[\mathbb{P}(D > k) = rac{m (s - 1)}{ms - 1} \cdot rac{(s - k)(s - k - 1)}{s (s - 1)} = rac{m \, (s - k)(s - k - 1)}{s \, (ms - 1)} .\]

entry.title: Three Bags of Coins
entry.content:
Problem.

There are three bags, each holding plenty of gold coins. Within a bag all coins weigh the same, and every weight is a positive integer number of grams. You have an exact electronic scale with unlimited range. In each weighing you may take any finite number of coins (possibly zero) from each bag, read the total weight, and use the result to decide the next weighing.

The following questions are independent. In each one, find the minimum number of weighings, and explain the method and the reason.

  1. One bag’s coins weigh $9$ or $11$ grams; the other two bags’ coins weigh $10$ grams. Find the abnormal bag and whether its coins are light or heavy.
  2. One bag’s coins differ from the other two by $1$ gram; the normal weight is unknown. Find the abnormal bag and whether its coins are light or heavy.
  3. Determine the per-coin weight of each of the three bags.

Solution.

Call the bags $A$, $B$, $C$ and write $w_A, w_B, w_C$ for the per-coin weights, all positive integers. A weighing with $a$ coins from $A$, $b$ from $B$ and $c$ from $C$ returns

\[S = a\,w_A + b\,w_B + c\,w_C .\]

The whole game is choosing $(a, b, c)$ so that $S$ decodes the unknowns. One lower bound is used throughout: zero weighings give no information, so whenever at least two states are possible, at least one weighing is needed.

Part 1: Take one, two and three coins

There are $3 \times 2 = 6$ states: which bag is abnormal, and whether it is light or heavy. Write $\delta \in {-1, +1}$ for the deviation and $x$ for the number of coins taken from the abnormal bag, so $x \in {a, b, c}$. Then

\[S = 10\,(a + b + c) + \delta x .\]

Take $(a, b, c) = (1, 2, 3)$: one coin from $A$, two from $B$, three from $C$. Then

\[S - 60 = \delta x \in \{-3, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3\},\]

and the six states give six different readings.

  • $S = 59, 58, 57$ means $A$, $B$, $C$ is light.
  • $S = 61, 62, 63$ means $A$, $B$, $C$ is heavy.

The sign of $S - 60$ says light or heavy, and its size says which bag. Any three distinct positive counts would work; $(0, 1, 2)$ would not, because $x = 0$ hides the deviation completely.

Since zero weighings cannot separate six states, the minimum is $1$ weighing.

Part 2: Make the unknown weight disappear modulo 7

Now the normal weight $w$ is an unknown positive integer, the abnormal bag weighs $w + \delta$ with $\delta \in {-1, +1}$, and a weighing gives

\[S = w\,(a + b + c) + \delta x, \qquad x \in \{a, b, c\} .\]

Look at the nuisance term. It is an unknown multiple of $N := a + b + c$, so it vanishes modulo $N$:

\[S \equiv \delta x \pmod N .\]

We therefore need the six residues $\pm a, \pm b, \pm c$ to be pairwise distinct modulo $N$. Conversely, if two different states have the same residue, write $\delta_1 x_1 - \delta_2 x_2 = kN$; then normal weights $w$ and $w + k$ (with $w$ large enough that both are at least $2$) give the same $S$, so distinctness is also necessary. The choice $(1, 2, 3)$ from Part 1 fails: $N = 6$ and $+3 \equiv -3 \pmod 6$, so “$C$ heavy with normal weight $w$” and “$C$ light with normal weight $w + 1$” both give $S = 6w + 3$ and cannot be told apart.

Take instead $(a, b, c) = (1, 2, 4)$, so $N = 7$.

  • $S \bmod 7 = 1, 2, 4$ means $A$, $B$, $C$ is heavy.
  • $S \bmod 7 = 6, 5, 3$ means $A$, $B$, $C$ is light.

All six residues are distinct, so one weighing decides both the bag and the direction. As a bonus, $w = (S - \delta x)/7$.

For example, if $w = 10$ and $C$ is light, then $S = 70 - 4 = 66 \equiv 3 \pmod 7$, which decodes correctly to “$C$, light”. Zero weighings is again impossible, so the minimum is $1$ weighing.

Six distinct classes $\pm a, \pm b, \pm c$ cannot fit in $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ for $N \leq 6$ when $a + b + c = N$, so $N \geq 7$ and $(1, 2, 4)$ even uses the fewest coins possible.

Part 3: One weighing is never enough

A single weighing with any $(a, b, c)$ shows one integer $S = a\,w_A + b\,w_B + c\,w_C$. Split on how many coefficients are positive.

  • If at least two coefficients are positive, say $a, b > 0$, then the distinct triples $(w_A + b, \; w_B, \; w_C)$ and $(w_A, \; w_B + a, \; w_C)$ give the same $S$.
  • If at most one coefficient is positive, two of the weights are never seen at all.

Either way $S$ cannot determine the triple $(w_A, w_B, w_C)$.

The obstruction is that the weights are unbounded: a fixed base like $(1, 10^3, 10^6)$ works only if $w_A$ and $w_B$ are known in advance to be below $10^3$. The way out is to let the first weighing produce a bound, and the second one exploit it.

Part 3: Two weighings, the first one picks the base

For the first weighing, take one coin from each bag:

\[S_1 = w_A + w_B + w_C .\]

Since all weights are positive integers, $1 \leq w_B, w_C \leq S_1 - 2 < S_1$.

For the second weighing, take one coin from $B$ and $S_1$ coins from $C$:

\[S_2 = w_B + S_1\,w_C .\]

Because $1 \leq w_B < S_1$, the pair $(w_B, w_C)$ is exactly the base-$S_1$ representation of $S_2$:

\[w_C = \left\lfloor \frac{S_2}{S_1} \right\rfloor, \qquad w_B = S_2 - S_1\,w_C, \qquad w_A = S_1 - w_B - w_C .\]

For example, if $(w_A, w_B, w_C) = (7, 12, 5)$, then $S_1 = 24$ and $S_2 = 12 + 24 \cdot 5 = 132$. Indeed $132 = 5 \cdot 24 + 12$, so $w_C = 5$, $w_B = 12$ and $w_A = 24 - 12 - 5 = 7$.

Two weighings suffice and one does not, so the minimum is $2$ weighings.

entry.title: Trailing Zeros of a Factorial
entry.content:
Problem.

How many consecutive zeros are there at the end of the decimal representation of $100!$?

Solution.

Start with small cases to see what is going on.

  • $4! = 24$ ends with no zero.
  • $5! = 120$ ends with one zero.
  • $10! = 3628800$ ends with two zeros.
  • $15! = 1307674368000$ ends with three zeros.

A new zero seems to appear every time we pass a multiple of $5$. That is the whole story, and the rest of this post explains why and how to count precisely.

A zero at the end is a factor of 10

A number ends with a zero exactly when it is divisible by $10$. It ends with two zeros exactly when it is divisible by $100 = 10^2$, and so on. So

\[\text{number of trailing zeros of } m = \text{the largest } k \text{ such that } 10^k \text{ divides } m .\]

Since $10 = 2 \cdot 5$, every factor $10$ is made of one factor $2$ and one factor $5$. Write the prime factorisation of $n!$ as

\[n! = 2^{a} \cdot 5^{b} \cdot (\text{primes other than } 2 \text{ and } 5) .\]

We can pair up one $2$ with one $5$ to make a $10$, and we can do this as many times as the scarcer of the two allows. So $n!$ is divisible by $10^{\min(a,b)}$, and after pulling those $10$’s out, what remains is missing either all its $2$’s or all its $5$’s, so it is not divisible by $10$ any more. Hence

\[\text{number of trailing zeros of } n! = \min(a, b) .\]

For $5! = 120 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ we have $a = 3$, $b = 1$, and indeed one zero.

There are always more 2’s than 5’s

Among the numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$, every second number is even, but only every fifth number is a multiple of $5$. So the factorial collects factors of $2$ much faster than factors of $5$: $a \geq b$ always. (The same comparison holds one level up: multiples of $4$ are more frequent than multiples of $25$, multiples of $8$ more frequent than multiples of $125$, and so on.)

Therefore $\min(a, b) = b$, and the problem becomes:

\[\text{number of trailing zeros of } n! = \text{number of factors } 5 \text{ in } n! .\]

We never have to think about $2$’s again.

Counting the 5’s in 100!

$100! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots 100$. Where do the factors $5$ come from?

  • Every multiple of $5$ contributes at least one factor $5$. Between $1$ and $100$ these are $5, 10, 15, \dots, 100$, which is $100 / 5 = 20$ numbers. That gives $20$ factors.
  • Some of these numbers contain the factor $5$ twice: the multiples of $25 = 5 \cdot 5$, namely $25, 50, 75, 100$. That is $100 / 25 = 4$ numbers. Each of them was already counted once above, so each contributes one more factor. That gives $4$ extra factors.
  • A number would contain the factor $5$ three times only if it were a multiple of $125 = 5^3$. But $125 > 100$, so there are none.

Adding up,

\[b = 20 + 4 + 0 = 24 .\]

Check the bookkeeping on one number: $50 = 2 \cdot 5^2$ has two factors $5$. It is counted once in the first bullet (as a multiple of $5$) and once in the second (as a multiple of $25$), total two. Correct. And $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ has one factor $5$; it is counted only in the first bullet. Correct.

For the record, the number of $2$’s is $a = 50 + 25 + 12 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 97$ (the same count with $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64$), far more than $24$. So

\[100! \text{ ends with exactly } 24 \text{ zeros.}\]

The general formula

Nothing above was special to $100$. For a general $n$:

  • $\lfloor n / 5 \rfloor$ numbers in ${1, \dots, n}$ are multiples of $5$: one factor each.
  • $\lfloor n / 25 \rfloor$ of them are multiples of $25$: one extra factor each.
  • $\lfloor n / 125 \rfloor$ of them are multiples of $125$: one more extra factor each.
  • And so on, until $5^k > n$, where the terms become $0$.

Here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ means “round down”. A number that contains the factor $5$ exactly $j$ times is a multiple of $5, 25, \dots, 5^j$ but not of $5^{j+1}$, so it is counted in exactly the first $j$ bullets, once each. So nothing is missed and nothing is double counted, and

\[\text{number of trailing zeros of } n! = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{5} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{25} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{125} \right\rfloor + \cdots\]

This is known as Legendre’s formula (for the prime $5$). For example, $n = 1000$ gives $200 + 40 + 8 + 1 = 249$ trailing zeros.

entry.title: A Review about Poisson Process – Forward and Backward Recurrence Times

link.title: A Review about Poisson Process – Forward and Backward Recurrence Times

entry.content:
Let ${N_t}_{t\geq 0}$ be a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda>0$, defined on a filtered probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$.

The $k$-th arrival time is defined by

\[T_k:=\inf\{t\geq 0:N_t\geq k\}, \qquad k\geq 1,\]

with

\[T_0:=0.\]

Since $N_t$ counts the number of arrivals up to time $t$, we have

\[N_t=\max\{k\geq 0:T_k\leq t\}.\]

1. Forward recurrence time

The time from $t$ until the next arrival is

\[W_t^+ := T_{N_t+1}-t.\]

We claim that

\[\boxed{ W_t^+\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda). }\]

Indeed, for any $x\geq 0$,

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(W_t^+>x) &= \mathbb{P}(T_{N_t+1}>t+x)\\ &= \mathbb{P}(N_{t+x}=N_t)\\ &= \mathbb{P}(N_{t+x}-N_t=0). \end{aligned}\]

By the stationary and independent increments of the Poisson process,

\[N_{t+x}-N_t\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda x).\]

Therefore,

\[\mathbb{P}(W_t^+>x) = e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x\geq 0.\]

Hence,

\[\boxed{ T_{N_t+1}-t\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda). }\]

This r.v. is called the forward recurrence time, forward waiting time, or residual waiting time.

2. Backward recurrence time

The time elapsed since the most recent arrival is

\[W_t^-:=t-T_{N_t}.\]

Here we use the convention $T_0=0$. Thus, if $N_t=0$, then

\[W_t^-=t.\]

For $0\leq x<t$, we have

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(W_t^->x) &= \mathbb{P}(t-T_{N_t}>x)\\ &= \mathbb{P}(N_t-N_{t-x}=0). \end{aligned}\]

Again, by stationary increments,

\[N_t-N_{t-x}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda x),\]

and therefore

\[\boxed{ \mathbb{P}(W_t^->x)=e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad 0\leq x<t. }\]

However, because the process starts at time $0$, there is a boundary effect. In particular,

\[\mathbb{P}(W_t^-=t) = \mathbb{P}(N_t=0) = e^{-\lambda t}.\]

Thus, the distribution function of $W_t^-$ is

\[\mathbb{P}(W_t^-\leq x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x<0,\\[4pt] 1-e^{-\lambda x}, & 0\leq x<t,\\[4pt] 1, & x\geq t. \end{cases}\]

In other words, $W_t^-$ has density

\[f_{W_t^-}(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad 0\leq x<t,\]

together with a point mass

\[\mathbb{P}(W_t^-=t)=e^{-\lambda t}.\]

This r.v. is called the backward recurrence time, or the age of the process at time $t$.

entry.title: Gambler’s Ruin
entry.content:
Problem.

A gambler starts with $i$ dollars and on each game wins a dollar with probability $p$ or loses one with probability $q = 1-p$, where $0 < p < 1$. He stops on reaching $N$ dollars or on losing everything. What is the probability that he ends up with $N$?

Solution.

Writing $P_i$ for that probability,

\[P_i = egin{cases}\dfrac{1-(q/p)^{\,i}}{1-(q/p)^{\,N}}, & p eq q, \[2ex] \dfrac{i}{N}, & p = q = frac12 .\end{cases}\]

Method 1: The difference equation

Condition on the first game,

\[P_i = p\,P_{i+1} + q\,P_{i-1}, \qquad 1 \le i \le N-1, \qquad P_0 = 0, \quad P_N = 1 .\]

The step that makes this easy is to write the left side as $(p+q)P_i$ and rearrange, which puts consecutive differences in a fixed ratio:

\[p\left(P_{i+1}-P_i ight) = q\left(P_i-P_{i-1} ight), \qquad ext{that is}\qquad P_{i+1}-P_i = rac{q}{p}\left(P_i-P_{i-1} ight) .\]

So the differences are geometric. Since $P_0 = 0$ the first of them is $P_1$, giving $P_i - P_{i-1} = (q/p)^{\,i-1}P_1$, and summing telescopes to

\[P_i = P_1 \sum_{j=0}^{i-1}\left( rac{q}{p} ight)^{j} .\]

The condition $P_N = 1$ now fixes $P_1$. For $p eq q$ the two geometric sums divide to give the stated formula, and for $p = q$ every term of the sum is $1$, so $P_i = i P_1$ with $P_1 = 1/N$.

Method 2: A martingale

Let $ au$ be the first time the fortune $S_n$ reaches $0$ or $N$. Optional stopping needs to know that this happens at all, which is worth isolating.

Lemma. $ au < \infty$ almost surely, and in fact $\mathbb E[ au] \le N/p^{\,N} < \infty$.

Proof. Cut time into blocks of $N$ games. If the game is still running when a block begins, the fortune lies between $1$ and $N-1$, so $N$ consecutive wins would carry it above $N$; since it moves one dollar at a time it must land on $N$ first and stop. Whatever has happened before, a block consists of $N$ wins with probability $p^{\,N} > 0$, so

\[\mathbb P\left( au > (k+1)N ight) \le \left(1-p^{\,N} ight)\mathbb P\left( au > kN ight), \qquad ext{hence}\qquad \mathbb P\left( au > kN ight) \le \left(1-p^{\,N} ight)^{k} .\]

As $0 < p < 1$ the right side tends to $0$, so $ au$ is finite almost surely. The tail decays geometrically, and summing it gives $\mathbb E[ au] = \sum_{n\ge0}\mathbb P( au > n) \le N\sum_{k\ge0}(1-p^{\,N})^{k} = N/p^{\,N}$. $ lacksquare$

The bound is crude, but finiteness is all that is required.

When $p = q$ the fortune is itself a martingale. The stopped process $S_{n \wedge au}$ takes values in $[0,N]$ and $ au$ is finite by the lemma, so dominated convergence carries $i = \mathbb E\left[S_{n\wedge au} ight]$ to the limit and

\[i = \mathbb E\left[S_ au ight] = N P_i + 0 \cdot (1-P_i) \implies P_i = rac{i}{N} .\]

When $p eq q$ the fortune is no longer a martingale, but $(q/p)^{S_n}$ is:

\[\mathbb E\left[\left( frac{q}{p} ight)^{S_{n+1}} \,\middle|\, S_n ight] = \left( frac{q}{p} ight)^{S_n}\left(p \cdot frac{q}{p} + q \cdot frac{p}{q} ight) = \left( frac{q}{p} ight)^{S_n} ,\]

the bracket being $q+p=1$. Optional stopping then reads

\[\left( rac{q}{p} ight)^{i} = \left( rac{q}{p} ight)^{N} P_i + 1 - P_i ,\]

which rearranges to the same answer. All the work has moved into spotting the martingale, and $q/p$ is precisely the characteristic root of the difference equation above.

An unbounded opponent

Letting $N o \infty$,

\[P_i \longrightarrow egin{cases} 1 - (q/p)^{\,i}, & p > q, \ 0, & p \le q .\end{cases}\]

Against an opponent of unlimited means the gambler is ruined with certainty unless the game is favourable, a fair game included. At $p = frac12$ the chance of ever reaching $N$ is only $i/N$, so the ruin is slow but sure.

entry.title: An Ace Each
entry.content:
Problem.

Fifty-two cards are dealt at random to four players, thirteen each. What is the probability that every player receives an ace?

Solution.

Method 1: Place the aces one at a time

Regard the deal as fifty-two labelled seats, thirteen belonging to each player, into which the cards fall. The four aces then occupy four seats chosen uniformly at random among all sets of four, and the question is whether those seats belong to four different players.

Seat the aces in turn. The first goes anywhere. Of the fifty-one seats left, the thirty-nine outside the first ace’s player are the ones that keep the count going; then thirty-eight are barred and twenty-six of the remaining fifty are good; then only the thirteen seats of the last player will do, out of forty-nine. Hence

\[P = \frac{39}{51}\cdot\frac{26}{50}\cdot\frac{13}{49} = \frac{2197}{20825} .\]

Method 2: Count the deals

A deal assigns the fifty-two cards to four distinguishable hands of thirteen, and there are $\dfrac{52!}{(13!)^{4}}$ of them. A favourable deal is built by handing the four aces to the four players, in one of $4!$ ways, and splitting the forty-eight other cards into four groups of twelve, in one of $\dfrac{48!}{(12!)^{4}}$ ways. So

\[P = \frac{4!\,\dfrac{48!}{(12!)^{4}}}{\dfrac{52!}{(13!)^{4}}} = 4!\cdot\frac{48!}{52!}\left(\frac{13!}{12!}\right)^{4} = \frac{24 \cdot 13^{4}}{52\cdot51\cdot50\cdot49} = \frac{2197}{20825} .\]

entry.title: Head Then Tail
entry.content:
Problem.

Two players toss a fair coin alternately, $A$ first. The game stops the first time a head is immediately followed by a tail, and whoever tossed that tail wins. What is the probability that $A$ wins?

Solution.

$A$ wins with probability $\frac49$.

Method 1: Condition on the first toss

Since the game ends almost surely with exactly one winner, $P(B) = 1 - P(A)$. Split on $A$’s opening toss,

\[P(A) = \tfrac12 P(A \mid H) + \tfrac12 P(A \mid T) .\]

The tail case. A tail cannot start an $HT$, and there is no head before it to complete one, so an opening tail is as if the toss never happened and only the turn has changed. What follows is a fresh game with $B$ tossing first, which puts $B$ in exactly the position $A$ held at the start. So $A$ is now the second player, and

\[P(A \mid T) = 1 - P(A) .\]

The head case. After $A$’s head it is $B$’s turn with a head pending, and $A$’s chance from there is $P(A \mid H)$, so $B$’s is $1 - P(A \mid H)$. Split on $B$’s reply. If $B$ tosses a tail, which happens half the time, $B$ wins at once and $A$ gets nothing. If $B$ tosses a head, then $A$ is to toss with a head pending, which is precisely the position $B$ occupied a moment ago with the names exchanged, so $A$ now has what $B$ had, namely $1 - P(A \mid H)$. Hence

\[P(A \mid H) = \frac12 \cdot 0 + \frac12\left(1 - P(A \mid H)\right) \implies P(A \mid H) = \frac13 .\]

Combining. Substituting both into the split,

\[P(A) = \frac12 \cdot \frac13 + \frac12\left(1 - P(A)\right) \implies P(A) = \frac49 .\]

Method 2: Sum over the winning toss

Until the game ends the record must read

\[\underbrace{T \cdots T}_{a \ \ge\ 0} \ \underbrace{H \cdots H}_{b \ \ge\ 1} \ T ,\]

because once a head appears the next tail ends the game, so every tail before the last one precedes every head. The winning toss is number $a+b+1$, and $A$ makes it exactly when $a+b$ is even.

Each such record has probability $2^{-(a+b+1)}$. Writing $k = a+b$, the pairs with $a \ge 0$, $b \ge 1$ and $a+b=k$ number $k$, so the game ends on toss $k+1$ with probability $k\,2^{-(k+1)}$, and $\sum_{k\ge1} k\,2^{-(k+1)} = 1$ as it must. Keeping the even $k$ and writing $k = 2j$,

\[P(A) = \sum_{k \text{ even}} \frac{k}{2^{\,k+1}} = \frac12 \sum_{j\ge1} 2j \left(\frac14\right)^{j} = \frac12 \cdot \frac{2 \cdot \frac14}{\left(1-\frac14\right)^{2}} = \frac49 .\]

This route needs no symmetry argument and yields the whole distribution of the ending time along the way.

entry.title: Candies in a Jar
entry.content:
Problem.

You are taking out candies one by one from a jar that has 10 red candies, 20 blue candies, and 30 green candies in it. What is the probability that there are at least 1 blue candy and 1 green candy left in the jar when you have taken out all the red candies?

Solution.

Let $T_r$, $T_b$ and $T_g$ be the number that the last red, blue, and green candies are taken out respectively. To have at least 1 blue candy and 1 green candy left when all the red candies are taken out, we need to have $T_r < T_b$ and $T_r < T_g$. In other words, we want to derive

\[P\left(\left\{T_r < T_b\right\} \cap \left\{T_r < T_g\right\}\right) = P(T_r < T_b < T_g) + P(T_r < T_g < T_b)\]

Since each of the 60 candies are equally likely to be the last candy and among them 30 are green ones, we have

\[P(T_g = 60) = \frac{30}{60}.\]

Conditioned on $T_g = 60$, among the 30 red and blue candies, each candy is again equally likely to be the last candy and there are 20 blue candies, so

\[P(T_r < T_b \vert{} T_g = 60) = \frac{20}{30}\]

and

\[P(T_r < T_b < T_g) = \frac{30}{60} \times \frac{20}{30}.\]

Similarly, we have $P(T_r < T_g < T_b) = \frac{20}{60} \times \frac{30}{40}$. Hence,

\[P(T_r < T_b \cap T_r < T_g) = \frac{7}{12}.\]
